directions: There are 10 questions about what you explored, from differentiation to convection currents. Answer every question, and then submit.

displayedOptions.text: Three
Four
Six

items.feedback: Earth has four main layers. They are the crust, the mantle, the outer core, and the inner core.

omittedOptions.rationale: "Two" matches no layer model the lesson teaches or that students commonly hold, so it is the least plausible distractor. "Three" (treating the core as one layer) and "Six" (counting subdivisions as main layers) keep the two meaningful counting misconceptions.

items.stem: How many main layers does Earth have?

displayedOptions.text: Differentiation
Convection currents
Erosion

items.feedback: Differentiation is how the molten Earth separated into layers by density. Heavy metals sank and formed the core. Lighter materials rose and formed the mantle and crust.

omittedOptions.rationale: Transmission is a wave term from another unit, not a process that moves or sorts Earth materials, so students can reject it without understanding differentiation. Convection currents (another density-driven motion in this lesson) and Erosion (a familiar process that moves and sorts material by weight) keep the two meaningful confusions.

items.stem: Early Earth was molten, or melted. Heavy metals like iron and nickel sank to the center. What is this sorting process called?

displayedOptions.text: Dense materials are pulled by the magnetic field
Dense materials are always the hottest
Dense materials sink below less dense materials

items.feedback: Density decides the order. In the molten Earth, materials could move freely. The densest materials sank the deepest. The least dense materials rose to the surface.

omittedOptions.rationale: "Float to the top" contradicts the stem, which already says the densest materials ended up at the center, so it can be rejected by reading the question alone. The magnetic-field and temperature distractors keep plausible wrong causes.

items.stem: Why did the densest materials end up at Earth's center?

displayedOptions.text: It is the thickest and most dense layer
It is a liquid layer made of iron and nickel
It is a thin, brittle layer and the least dense

items.feedback: The crust is the thin, brittle outer layer. It is only 4 to 25 miles thick. It is the least dense layer, and it is the one we live on.

omittedOptions.rationale: C and D both give the crust a property of the outer core. C is kept because it also tests the crust's state (brittle solid, not liquid); D repeats the same wrong-layer confusion without testing state.

items.stem: Which sentence best describes the crust?

displayedOptions.text: Oceanic crust is thinner, younger, and more dense
Oceanic crust is thicker and less dense
Continental crust is thinner, younger, and made of basalt

items.feedback: Oceanic crust is made of basalt. It is about 4 miles thick on average, and it is younger and more dense. Continental crust is made of granite. It is about 25 miles thick on average, and it is older and less dense.

omittedOptions.rationale: "Exactly the same" is contradicted by the question itself, which compares two named crust types, and by the lesson ("Not all crust is the same"); its absolute wording also makes it easy to eliminate. A and C keep the two reversal misconceptions.

items.stem: A scientist compares oceanic crust with continental crust. Which sentence is true?

displayedOptions.text: It turns the crust into a liquid
It moves the plates above it
It stops earthquakes from happening

items.feedback: Temperature differences make the mantle flow slowly. The moving mantle makes Earth's plates move. Moving plates are what change the surface.

omittedOptions.rationale: "No effect on the surface" contradicts the stem, which says the flow matters for the surface, so it is eliminated by the question itself. B (flow means melting or liquid) and C (flow prevents earthquakes) keep the meaningful misconceptions.

items.stem: The mantle is solid rock, but it flows very slowly. Why is this important for Earth's surface?

displayedOptions.text: The asthenosphere
The lithosphere
The inner core

items.feedback: The asthenosphere is the part of the upper mantle that flows. This flowing quality is called plastic behavior. The asthenosphere is responsible for convection currents.

omittedOptions.rationale: Oceanic crust is part of the crust, which the lesson teaches is brittle solid rock, and the question asks for a layer that flows; its main lure is the everyday phrase "ocean currents". The lithosphere (the rigid layer taught as a pair with the asthenosphere) and the inner core (confusing the heat source with the flowing layer) keep the conceptual misconceptions.

items.stem: One layer flows like soft plastic. It is responsible for convection currents. Which layer is it?

displayedOptions.text: The pull of the Moon's gravity
Only the spinning of the inner core
Heat energy from deep inside Earth

items.feedback: Energy from inside Earth heats the rock. Hot rock rises, cools, and sinks. This loop is called a convection current. It keeps the mantle moving and moves the crust.

omittedOptions.rationale: Wind acts only on the surface and the air, so it is the easiest choice to reject for a current inside the mantle. The Moon's gravity (an outside force students know moves ocean water) and the spinning inner core (a wrong mechanism inside Earth) keep the meaningful misconceptions.

items.stem: What causes the convection currents in the mantle?

displayedOptions.text: The released energy reverses Earth's magnetic field
Energy shakes the crust as an earthquake
A new continent forms right away

items.feedback: When stuck plates finally slip, the built-up pressure is released. It moves out as energy that shakes the crust. That shaking is an earthquake.

omittedOptions.rationale: Owner review: "the inner core melts" is too disconnected from plates getting stuck, pressure building, and sudden release. It is omitted. Canonical r1 has no other distractor about releasing plate pressure, so A is kept and its wording states the misconception as an effect of the release; its canonical meaning (the magnetic field reverses) is unchanged.

items.stem: Plates usually slide smoothly. Sometimes they get stuck, and pressure builds up. What happens when the pressure is suddenly released?

displayedOptions.text: The crust moves on its own and is not connected to the deeper layers
The magnetic field made deep in Earth's core causes earthquakes and volcanoes
Heat drives convection in the mantle, which moves plates and causes earthquakes and volcanoes

items.feedback: Heat deep inside Earth drives convection currents in the mantle. That flow moves the plates. The moving plates cause earthquakes and volcanoes at the surface. Earth's inner layers and their energy explain changes at the surface.

omittedOptions.rationale: A (only weather changes the surface) and C (the crust moves with no link to deeper layers) both deny that the interior causes surface change. C is kept because it also reflects a plate-motion misconception (the crust moves by itself), closer to this lesson's causal chain; D keeps a wrong internal mechanism (the magnetic field).

items.stem: Which sentence best explains how Earth's inner layers cause changes at the surface?

showYourThinking.modelAnswer: Earth's core is extremely hot, and that heat rises into the mantle. The mantle is solid rock, but it flows slowly. Hot rock is less dense, so it rises. Cooler rock is more dense, so it sinks. This loop of rising and sinking rock is called convection. Convection currents drag the plates on top, so the plates move. Moving plates can get stuck, and pressure builds up. When they suddenly slip, the energy shakes the crust as an earthquake. In some places where plates meet or pull apart, rock deep below melts into magma, or molten rock. The magma can rise and erupt from volcanoes. If your steps go from the hot core to mantle convection to plate motion to surface change, you have it.
showYourThinking.prompt: Explain how Earth's inner layers cause earthquakes and volcanoes at the surface. Write one or two sentences. Name the steps in order, starting with the hot core. Do not just list the layers. Use the word convection.
